Not Recommended
170.0 hrs on record
Posted: August 13
This game has so much to like about it. It's pretty well designed with 5 of the 6 classes having interesting abilities and builds. It even has fun little alternatives thrown in from time to time so you aren't looking at the exact same battles over and over. Even though it's an idle battler, it's still fun to watch it and tinker with your team to make it better. So what's the problem then? Well, you're going to have a hard time ever getting to play those interesting builds. At some point the game stops being so forgiving about what gear you're wearing and what skills you've invested in and you will stop progressing unless you start putting together abilities and a party with synergy. No big deal, we'll just start being more intentional with what things we pick...except, you can't. Every element of getting stronger is blocked behind 100 layers of RNG. You will spend an entire day getting what looks like an outrageous amount of resources and you'll spend it all in less than 5 minutes rolling dice trying to get what you want/need and just end up with nothing but a wasted day. It's a miserable feeling, and unfortunately one that overshadows all the great things this game could be.

EDIT: I wish there was a better review system rather than just thumbs up/down, because just a "negative" feels unfair to the work that's been put in. I stand by my frustrated feeling of wasting the entire day's idle farming in an instant without getting any stronger, but the dev(s) are very active with updates and do seem like they want you to have more agency in your gameplay. If you are reading my review, please do not take this as "this game sucks, stay away". Instead, take it as a warning that if you're the type that likes to experiment with build ideas, this very early version of the game will give you a lot of frustrations trying to do that. Based on the way daily game updates have trended I think eventually my review will be changed to a positive one, but for now I'm leaving it where it is.

A real shame the demo was taken down for release as it did a great job of giving you an idea of how the game would be since the first six chapters were included. That being said, the game is quite addicting and enjoyable so far. The first 5 chapters feel very well paced and reward you at every tiny milestone to keep the progression going through early game. It starts to slow down quite a bit around chapter 6 (at least for me), but by then you have a strong foundation of the gameplay loop, how to get stronger, how to get better gear, and so on.

The core gameplay loop is "bewitching" (buying/recruiting) units to your pool of Godsworn dudes, adding them to slots in the combat window, and letting them auto battle through the stages to complete chapters. As stages are completed, rewards are given, which are used to make numbers go up. I typically don't really enjoy this kind of system so could never get into POE/Diablo but here it's very enjoyable since you don't have to actively press buttons on really repetitive stages over and over to get your loot. You tab back in every so often, open your chests and see what you got.

Gear can be bought at the shop or gotten in chest drop rewards where stats roll randomly which is where the loot goblin-ing addiction occurs. There are also alternative categories of stages that serve as targeted resource farms which help with progression a bit as well. You can also forge to improve base stats on items you already have or socket runes in to add a little extra. The inventory also has a filtering system to autosell drops based on parameters you decide to make management a little less repetitive.

The game does a pretty good job of helping you navigate through the various menus with its basic but serviceable tutorial popups. Descriptions for currencies are generally well described and help you quickly understand what things are used for and how to get more if that is your current bottleneck. Currencies also passively generated over time and even generate offline as well which feels pretty standard these days. You can even minimize the game which makes it turn into a little floating overlay on your computer so you can do other stuff and glance at progress every so often.

The story is non-existant and the music is mostly forgettable but does its job. The art style is goofy and charming albeit shamelessly ripped off of Darkest Dungeon and a lot of WoW gear.

My main criticisms are some of the UI behavior and some of the game design. For UI, I wished clicking away from a particular menu minimized it automatically because there are way too many instances where windows overlap on each other and it becomes a pain in the ass to do things cause you have to go hit the X button on one side of the screen cause it's covering part of a menu on the other side. Some text wrapping issues are there which makes some tooltips unreadable. Effects are pretty poorly described. For example, everybody knows "crit" but what does that mean in context of this game? There is a manual thing in game that describes some things but it's very barebones and doesn't even have all the effects. Design wise, having the Godsworn have different rarities that affect scaling effectively make anyone that rolls not rare/yellow immediately useless. It becomes a chore quickly of leveling guys, having money, and trying to roll for new guys that have better stat scaling because they're more rare. It then also becomes annoying to have to relevel those same guys cause they are recruited at a lower level than your party currently is.

There is also a re-roll system for skills on your dudes but it's a bit bizarre since it only rolls certain skills, is random which skills you already have gets rerolled, and has a chance of rolling into a new skill that is "locked" which prevents it from being rerolled unless you use an item to unlock it. It makes trying to build what you want a bit of a pain and also makes you not want to interact with the system cause it might reroll a skill you've already invested time and effort into building around. You can reset your points to put into the new skills but it costs currency to do so which makes it feel restrictive. I don't mind a bit of friction in design, but I feel like the friction shouldn't be designed in such a way to discourage players from experimenting or even interacting with a particular mechanic.

Lastly, they also neglected to put the AI content disclaimer on the page pre-release so I didn't even even realize until writing this which is a bit of a bummer but whatever.

Complaints aside, I think it's still a fun game, especially at such a cheap price. If you're getting home from work and don't have the mental/physical energy to play something active but still want to enjoy some kind of game it's the perfect relaxer and de-stresser. We'll see how things are in late game when the honeymoon phase has worn off.

Update 1: I've passed the Ch. 10 wall (where you get the third row of combat) and would wholeheartedly recommend the game. Everything feels very well designed and thought out in design minus the skill reroll system (which the devs patched very quickly so they listen to feedback!) which now feels excellent after the change. The grind of catching up newly recruited Godsworn is mitigated by the Sanctum permanent adventure bonus buffs (one of which is permanent exp gain increase) which could maybe be tuned in numbers a bit to be slightly higher but feels well designed in concept. Set Items and Legendary Items you don't need still feel rewarding to get because of the Market Order system that gives the skill reroll lock/unlock item so every drop feels exciting even if it doesn't directly benefit your current party setup. As you progress, the enemies change up their setups/damage types enough that you have a difficult time using just one strat repeatedly which encourages getting new Godsworn to cover your weaknesses and adds just enough friction to be very engaging with the Godsworn recruitment reroll system feeling problem-solvey without being too frustrating. However if you don't want to, you can embrace the spirit of idle game and just level your guys level over time to brute force your way through with stats with patience. You almost always feel like you have agency as a player to solve the current problem. The only major complaint I feel still remains valid is UI issues/translations and conveying more information to the player about what stats do or how they work. The rest is extremely minor things that can be adjusted with number changes such as Abyssal Scale and Resonance Crystal drop rates so the player can better/more consistently target farm the resources they need to deal with the challenges. The core framework is fantastic and I'm looking forward to seeing how the game evolves over time.

Path of Exile, but for people with a mortgage and a job

Do not let the word idle fool you. This is not a casual game where you look at a cookie and tap your screen. This is pure, unadulterated ARPG spreadsheet math. It takes the absolute best parts of Path of Exile, the ruthless min-maxing, the massive build variety, and the obsessive gear tinkering, and removes the part where you get carpal tunnel from clicking a billion times The developers clearly understood the dark fantasy assignment.

Instead of running around maps for twelve hours to fix your resistances, you spend your time staring at gear prefixes, suffixes, and runewords to craft the ultimate automated killing machine. You will find yourself genuinely stressing over a fractional percentile difference on an elemental resistance roll just to push your cultists through the next dimension

10 of 10, the only issue i found is that it ends. and i desperately want more

Please, if you are a casual person that doesn't want to think a lot about itemization, this game ISNT FOR YOU.

Most people i see with negative reviews state that the game has unnecessary complexity when it comes to stats, but the stats are fine in my opinion.

Developer, if you read this please just add an explanation on what runewords do exactly because it isn't intuitive.

Game is perfectly fine and should scratch an itch for people who like PoE/Diablo2 Itemization and the depth that comes attached to it and autobattler/idles

The game is idle but you have to min max a lot so you have windows of activity and idleness, at least where i'm at in the progression curve that's the case.

The bad: We desperately need a Search bar in the warehouse and inventory and a more robust filter.

Another very bad thing about the game is that they shower you with uniques (items with ability/passive/drastic statistical changing abilities) and set effects (same thing but only activates once you have an arbitrary number of items of the same set VERY EARLY ON, making rare items kind of subpar and uninteresting when i was still gettingg accustomed to the affixes that can augment said items.

Sadly this is a very big problem in games with rarity item-caste systems nowadays since devs of the 2020's are seemingly afraid of making rare drops actually rare, underestimating the oomph of a truly rare item, this just makes us read way too many things, and when the dupes of dupes of dupes of something that should have been special hit it just doesn't feel good.

Just give us access to affix editing in some way that progressively gets better and just make legendaries really rare.

If they had nailed that maybe this would be an 8/10 game.

As small as a puddle, as deep as an ocean, you could say.

There's not much to do but focus on your bewitched prisoners to increase their level/stats to keep venturing through the "campaign".
The problem is that there are so many attributes and so many stats but little to no helpful information on what scales on what.

You can have an Archer that can equip both a bow and a dagger. Do both scale from dex, or daggers from physical? Or both? And he's got a skill that does lightning damage, is that Magic damage? Do I need Intelligence now too? It doesn't explain anything.
There's so many stats on equipment and no way to find out if it's better than what you've currently got equipped.

So, if you like creating spreadsheets to find out which skill will benefit most of which attribute, or which items is better for your current build, go for it.
I find it confusing and I'm pretty sure after the first hour you've seen all there is to find in this game and it just becomes a rinse and repeat to min/max your parties, which is not for me.

The game is okay overall. Some build are just so much better than other and it's not even close. The game is balanced around just going glass canon because they have a system that punish defensive build. You take more damage as the battle goes on and this debuff can stack so there's no reason to build tank at all. The game overall feels pretty limited, there isn't much combination you can go with because of the system they made to punish you.

The class balance does not feel good. Warrior class are just so much stronger through all stages and game mode of the game. They scale so well into the end game and just bypass the game damage reduction mechanics in some game modes because they scale so well. Mercenary class is just completely useless and the weakest for all stages and game modes, it's almost counter productive to use this class at anytime. Cleric, hunter, priest, and mage are all reasonably good. To solve all the problem for the game, you just build two offensive warrior and priest to complete the game. Some classes/builds just don't scale even when you add the combination of the passive skills together even with from other classes, runeword and mutations.

If they want to make the game better, they need to change the fatigue system or counter balance the fatigue system with overtime scaling to do more damage overtime. The fatigue system makes your characters take more damage by 10% per stack the longer the fight goes on. If your DPS classes doesn't do more damage overtime, then there's no reason to build a defensive character because longer battles is just punishment. Also, DPS warriors are so strong, they also tank better than defensive build characters so there's no reason to ever have a defensive build for any of the classes if you are trying to push progression.

The game and the logic of the game do not feels like 1.0 game, more like 0.9 and need some changes to make other classes relevant by tweeking the system and/or have better scaling/passive for those classes. They also need to add more stages for doom and/or make class restriction. Right now, you can just use priest and warriors team to clear all of the doom stages easily. This is true for outlands as well. It's one of the just put all the blocks in the circle since every shape of blocks can fit inside the circle.

Since Steam only offers Recommend or Not Recommend, I'm currently leaning toward Not Recommend due to game balance issues and several design choices that did not align with my expectations.

That said, this does not mean the game is bad. The developers are active and continuously updating the game. At the time of this review, they have already added numerous quality-of-life improvements, which shows their commitment to supporting the game.

One of my main concerns is that the game doesn't feel like a true idle game. I would describe it as roughly 50% idle and 50% active management. If you're looking for something that can mostly play itself, this may not be the game for you. Team compositions that work perfectly in one stage can suddenly become ineffective in another, forcing you to constantly rethink synergies and adjust your setup.

Fortunately, the community is very helpful and provides guides for progression. Without those guides, it can take quite a while to figure out certain strategies on your own.

Another aspect I didn't enjoy was the item RNG. Both item stats and effects are randomized, which can significantly impact your build. I often found myself spending more time optimizing equipment, skills, and team compositions than actually letting the game idle.

To finish the game, you'll generally need at least three different team compositions, which conveniently matches the game's limit of three saved setups. Personally, I wish the game allowed more team slots so players could experiment with additional builds. In my experience, one setup is used primarily for farming gear and resources, while the other two are tailored for specific encounters and progression requirements, particularly during later stages such as the "Doom" levels. Depending on the challenge, you'll frequently switch between compositions.

I also wish there was a speed modifier such as 2x game speed, as some battles can feel quite slow. Progression farming is generally done on higher stages, but you can't invest purely into damage because glass-cannon builds tend to struggle with survivability. Balancing offense and defense is often necessary.

Despite these criticisms, the game does several things very well.

There are six different classes, and the recruitment system offers flexibility. Instead of endlessly refreshing for the perfect recruit, you can invest resources to improve unit quality through a gambling-style upgrade system. While resource-intensive, it provides a meaningful use for excess materials. If you prefer less manual management, the game also offers automatic refreshing until your desired class or rarity appears. Similar automation exists in the shop, making purchasing less dependent on random drops.

Another positive is the inclusion of recommended builds for players who need guidance. While there are definitely meta strategies that make progression easier, having in-game recommendations helps newer players get started.

The skill system is also enjoyable because it allows rerolling skills to better fit the build you're trying to create, giving players more control over character development.

Final Thoughts

Overall, if you're comfortable actively managing builds, adjusting team compositions, and optimizing gear from time to time, this is a decent game worth considering. However, players expecting a highly automated idle experience may be disappointed.

My biggest issues are the heavy reliance on item RNG, the need to frequently adapt to meta compositions, and the amount of micromanagement required. Ironically, once you've completed the game, that's when you're finally free to fully experiment with different builds, but by then you've already seen most of what the game has to offer.

Pros

Active developers with frequent updates
Strong quality-of-life improvements
Six unique classes
Helpful automation features
Build recommendations for new players
Skill reroll system adds flexibility

Cons

Doesn't feel like a true idle game
Heavy reliance on team composition and meta strategies
Significant item RNG
Only three composition slots
No speed-up option
Requires frequent optimization and micromanagement

Verdict: Decent game with good progression systems and developer support, but not ideal for players looking for a mostly hands-off idle experience.

I finished the whole game and got 100% of the achievements.

Worth $12? Sure! That said, I had higher expectations for the game overall.

I really liked the variety of builds, and for a good portion of my playthrough, the difficulty felt pretty satisfying. There were several points where I genuinely had to work to get past difficulty spikes and improve my build.

Unfortunately, successive patches seemed to make the game easier and easier, to the point where most of the content became very easy to steamroll. You could even see the difference in how many more players started getting the endgame achievements.

I also really liked the original idea behind the endgame: taking one of your characters on a difficult solo adventure. Doom apparently ended up being hard to balance, though, and the latest patch has scrapped the idea of solo runs.

Overall, I enjoyed my time with the game and definitely got my $12 worth, but I think it lost some of what made the progression and endgame satisfying along the way.
